questions.stem: Evelyn, 16, tells you in the ED, "I just can't stop throwing up. I think I've got gastro." She is breathing deeply and quickly but is alert. You have a few minutes of focused history. Which question is most likely to uncover the underlying diagnosis?
options: Have you had any diarrhoea, and has anyone at home been sick?
Is the pain worse if I press on the lower right side of your tummy?
Have you been thirstier, or weeing more often, over the last few weeks?
Have you had any headache, or any trouble with your vision?
questions.why: Adolescents rarely mention polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia or weight loss unless asked. Vomiting plus these osmotic symptoms means DKA until proven otherwise, so check a bedside glucose and ketones early.
notes: Worth asking to test her gastro theory, but a negative answer only makes gastro less likely. It does not point to the actual cause.
Screens for appendicitis, which doesn't fit her mild generalised soreness and wouldn't explain the deep, fast breathing.
Screens for raised intracranial pressure as a cause of vomiting, but it doesn't target the osmotic symptoms that point to DKA.

questions.stem: Evelyn, 16, weighs about 52 kg and has severe DKA (glucose 38.2 mmol/L, pH 7.05, HCO3 4, ketones 6.0, K 5.3). Her 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus has been given, and deficit fluids with potassium are running. Which insulin plan is most appropriate?
options: IV insulin bolus 0.1 units/kg, then an infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h
IV infusion 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h, started about 1 h after fluids, no bolus
Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin 0.1 units/kg every 2 hours
IV infusion 0.1 units/kg/h, stopped once glucose falls below 15 mmol/L
questions.why: Paediatric DKA guidelines (RCH, ISPAD) use an IV insulin infusion of 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h, started about an hour after fluids, with no bolus. A bolus speeds the falls in glucose, osmolality and potassium and may add to the risk of cerebral oedema.
notes: An insulin bolus is not recommended in paediatric DKA. It increases the risk of hypokalaemia and of rapid osmotic shifts.
Subcutaneous insulin is not appropriate in severe DKA with dehydration. Absorption is unreliable and the dose can't be adjusted hour by hour.
Insulin is needed until the ketosis clears. When glucose falls below about 15 mmol/L you add 5% glucose to the fluids and keep the insulin running.

questions.stem: Evelyn, 16, has severe DKA after 3 weeks of osmotic diuresis and a day of vomiting, yet her serum potassium is 5.3 mmol/L. Her normal ECG is a baseline before insulin starts. Which mechanism mainly explains why her serum potassium will fall quickly once the insulin infusion starts?
options: Insulin stimulates Na+/K+-ATPase, moving K+ into muscle and liver cells
Insulin raises aldosterone, increasing K+ secretion in the collecting duct
Insulin increases albumin binding of K+, lowering the free plasma fraction
Insulin blocks proximal tubular K+ reabsorption, causing a kaliuresis
questions.why: Without insulin, and with acidosis, potassium shifts out of cells, so the serum level looks normal or high even though total body potassium is depleted. Insulin switches on Na+/K+-ATPase and drives K+ back into cells, so serum K can fall fast. That is why potassium goes into the fluids once K is below 5.5.
notes: Insulin doesn't act mainly through aldosterone. The fall in K+ is a shift into cells, not a sudden rise in renal loss.
Potassium isn't meaningfully protein-bound. Albumin binding matters for calcium, not potassium.
Insulin doesn't block proximal tubular K+ handling. The fast fall comes from K+ moving into cells, not from urinary loss.

questions.stem: Six hours into DKA treatment, Evelyn, 16, complains of a worsening headache and becomes drowsy. Her heart rate falls to 58 and her BP rises. Her right pupil is now dilated and reacts sluggishly to light. Compression of which structure best explains the pupil sign?
options: Right abducens nerve, stretched over the petrous temporal apex
Right cervical sympathetic chain, within the carotid sheath
Left optic tract, near the lateral geniculate body
Right oculomotor nerve, compressed by the uncus at the tentorial edge
questions.why: Cerebral oedema can push the medial temporal lobe (uncus) through the tentorial notch, compressing the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve. Its parasympathetic pupillary fibres run on the outside of the nerve, so a dilated, sluggish pupil appears early. This is an emergency: give mannitol or hypertonic saline at once.
notes: Abducens stretch is a false localising sign. It causes lateral rectus weakness with a convergent squint, not a dilated pupil.
Loss of sympathetic supply causes Horner's syndrome, with a small pupil (miosis) and ptosis, not a dilated one.
An optic tract lesion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, not a unilateral dilated, sluggish pupil.
